pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 6-7 (Y2). Understand that the two digits of a two-digit number represent amounts of TENS and ONES: in 47, the 4 means 4 tens (40) and the 7 means 7 ones. This is the central node of early place value — the tens/ones column idea that every later place-value column extends.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y2): 'recognise the place value of each digit in a two-digit number (tens, ones)'; 'identify, represent and estimate numbers using different representations, including the number line'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.NBT.2 'understand that the two digits of a two-digit number represent amounts of tens and ones' with 1.NBT.2a/b/c; consolidated in 2.NBT.1.
• Operational details — Build every two-digit number CONCRETELY first (bundled tens + loose ones), then match to the written numeral and to expanded form (47 = 40 + 7). Insist the child reads the tens digit as a QUANTITY OF TENS, not the face value ('four tens', not 'four'). Contrast standard partition (47 = 40 + 7) with non-standard partition (47 = 30 + 17) once secure, because flexible partitioning underpins later column addition/subtraction.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 6): with base-ten blocks present, build 47 and say '4 tens and 7 ones'. Tier B (age 6-7): given 47 with no blocks, state the value of each digit (40 and 7) and write 47 = 40 + 7. Tier C (age 7): identify the tens/ones digit in any two-digit number and give a non-standard partition (47 = 30 + 17).
bestPractices: Follow the CPA sequence: bundle ten loose ones into a labelled 'ten' (concrete), draw it as a ten-rod/line (pictorial), then link to the numeral 47 and expanded form 40+7 (abstract) — never leave the digit floating free of a quantity.
Use a place-value chart with only two columns (tens | ones) and physically place bundled tens in the tens column and loose ones in the ones column so the position IS the meaning.
Read the digits by value out loud — '4 tens' and '7 ones' — and resist 'four, seven'; language that names the unit prevents the digits-are-just-two-separate-numbers error.
Introduce non-standard partitioning (47 = 30 + 17) deliberately once standard partitioning is secure, so children see the tens/ones split as flexible, not a single fixed answer.
Use 'the same number, many ways' tasks: show 47 as blocks, as 40+7, as a point on a 0-100 line, and as a bead string of 4 tens + 7 — same quantity, different representation.
keyRepresentations: Base-ten blocks (tens rods + unit cubes) — the canonical proportional model where a ten is physically ten ones
Two-column tens|ones place-value chart with bundled tens and loose ones placed in position
Expanded-form / part-whole (cherry) diagram: 47 splits into 40 and 7
Bead strings and ten-frames grouped into complete tens plus extras
Arrow/place-value cards (40 and 7) that physically overlap to build 47, making expanded form tangible
commonMisconceptions: Reading the tens digit as its face value — treating the 4 in 47 as 'four' rather than 'forty/four tens'.
Concatenation error: thinking 47 is '4 and 7' side by side (so 4+7=11 or two separate numbers) rather than 40+7.
Digit-reversal / transposition — writing or building 74 for 47 because spoken language and column order are conflated (a hangover from the teen-number naming trap).
Believing a number can only be partitioned one way (47 = 40 + 7 only), missing 47 = 30 + 17, which blocks later regrouping in subtraction.
Losing the unit when there are zero ones — thinking a decade like 40 has 'no place value in the ones' rather than 4 tens and 0 ones.

learn.summary: For ages 6-7 (Y2 / US Grade 1-2), build the understanding that the two digits of a two-digit number stand for a quantity of tens and a quantity of ones: in 47, the 4 means 4 tens (40) and the 7 means 7 ones. Centre the learning on concrete grouping — bundling ten loose ones into one ten — then link that quantity to the written numeral, to expanded form (47 = 40 + 7), and to flexible (non-standard) partitioning (47 = 30 + 17). Read digits by value ('four tens', 'seven ones'), never as bare faces.

activities.title: Bundling: ten ones become one ten
feedback: If the child says 'the 4 means four', have them count the single cubes inside the four bundles: there are forty, so the 4 is worth 4 tens = 40.

If the child places tens in the ones column (or vice versa), name the columns again — tens on the left, ones on the right — and compare 47 with 74 built side by side so the positions are visibly different quantities.
When partitioning as 30 + 17, confirm by re-counting the whole pile: if it is still 47, the split is valid; the quantity is conserved even though the grouping changed.
If the child thinks a decade like 40 has 'nothing' in the ones, show 40 as four tens and zero loose ones — the ones place is still there, holding none.
activities.rationale: Place value is a quantity re-seen as grouped units. Acting out the bundling (ten ones fusing into one ten) makes unitising something the child does rather than a label they repeat, which is the standard concrete-first (CPA) route and is intended to target the face-value and concatenation errors.
sourceClaims: 1.NBT.2 states the two digits of a two-digit number represent amounts of tens and ones, with 10 as a bundle of ten ones.
Explicit CPA (concrete-pictorial-abstract) sequencing and standard/non-standard partitioning are recommended for building place-value understanding.
learnerActions: Set out a two-column mat labelled 'tens' on the left and 'ones' on the right.
Drop loose cubes one at a time into the ones column; each time you reach ten loose cubes, bundle those ten into a single labelled 'ten' (a rod) and move it to the tens column.
Build 47 by placing four bundled tens in the tens column and seven loose ones in the ones column.
Say aloud 'four tens and seven ones', then write the numeral 47 and the expanded form 47 = 40 + 7.
Break one of the four tens back into ten loose ones and re-count: show the pile is still 47 but now reads as 30 + 17.
activities.intendedInsight: The '4' in 47 is not 'four' — it is four whole bundles of ten (40). Position gives the digit its value, and the same quantity can be split in more than one way without changing how much there is.

activities.title: Many ways to show the same number
feedback: If the child marks 47 near the wrong end of the line, count up in tens (10, 20, 30, 40) then on by ones to locate it.
For 44, if the child says both 4s mean the same, point to the place of each: the left 4 sits in the tens column (40), the right 4 in the ones column (4).
If the child drops the ones place for 40, have them state it as '4 tens and 0 ones' to keep the place visible.
If the arrow cards are read as '4' and '7', separate then re-overlap them so the '40' card is seen whole underneath the '7'.
activities.rationale: Linking multiple representations of one quantity is intended to build the flexible, connected understanding named in the Y2 standard, including representing numbers on a number line, and guards against treating each representation as a separate fact.
sourceClaims: Y2 pupils should recognise the place value of each digit in a two-digit number (tens, ones) and identify/represent/estimate numbers using different representations including the number line.
learnerActions: Take one number, e.g. 47, and represent it several ways: as bundled tens + loose ones, as expanded form 40 + 7, as a part-whole (cherry) diagram with 47 at the top splitting into 40 and 7, as a point marked at 47 on a 0-100 number line, as a bead string of 4 tens plus 7 beads, and by overlapping arrow/place-value cards (a '40' card with a '7' card sliding over it to read 47).
Check that every representation is the same quantity by counting back to 47 each time.
Repeat with a decade number such as 40 and with a number containing a repeated digit such as 44, explaining why the two 4s in 44 are worth different amounts (40 and 4).
activities.intendedInsight: A number is a single quantity that can be shown in many different ways; the tens/ones meaning stays the same across blocks, numerals, expanded form, the part-whole diagram, arrow cards, and the number line.

activities.title: Convince me the 4 means forty
feedback: Accept any justification that ties the digit to its place and counts the underlying ones (four tens = forty).
If the child only restates 'it's forty because it is', ask them to point to and count the actual tens to ground the claim.
Treat this as a short follow-up after concrete building, not a substitute for it — the child's reasoning can then be tied to bundles they have actually handled.
activities.rationale: A brief reasoning prompt may surface whether the child attaches the digit to its place or is reciting; it is proposed to work best as consolidation after hands-on grouping rather than as the first encounter, since the concept is grounded in manipulating quantities. Discussion alone can elicit an explanation but does not itself provide the physical grouping.
learnerActions: Respond to the challenge: 'Convince me the 4 in 47 is worth forty, not four.'
Justify using a model you built — e.g. 'because the 4 is four bundles, and each bundle is ten, so that is forty.'
Extend to a prove-it task: 'Show that the two 4s in 44 are worth different amounts.'
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to explain and defend why a digit's value comes from its place cements the idea beyond stating the rule.

activities.title: Check and sort by place value
feedback: For a swap error, rebuild 47 and 74 side by side so the different tens counts are visible.
For 4 + 7 = 11, show that the digits are not added together; the 4 counts tens and the 7 counts ones, giving 40 + 7 = 47.
For 47 = 30 + ___, confirm the missing part is 17 by regrouping one ten into ten ones.
For 47 = ___ + 7, confirm the missing part is 40 (four tens).
activities.rationale: Targeted checks that include the two headline distractors (transposition, 74, and adding the digits at face value, 11) can confirm the idea is held and probe the specific misconceptions. A check or sort can classify and verify a child's answers but does not itself elicit the physical grouping, so pair it with the building activity.
learnerActions: Choose which picture shows 4 tens and 7 ones, and match written numerals to their block pictures.
Sort or state, for a given two-digit number, which digit is the tens digit and which is the ones digit, and the value of each.
Consider tempting wrong answers — e.g. 74 (digits swapped) and 11 (adding 4 + 7) — and explain why each is wrong.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure recall that each digit's value is fixed by its place, and conscious rejection of the swap error (74) and the digit-adding/face-value error (11, from adding 4 + 7).

constraints: Always build a two-digit number concretely first (bundled tens + loose ones), then connect it to the numeral and expanded form; never leave a digit floating free of a quantity.
Read digits by unit aloud — 'four tens', 'seven ones' — not 'four, seven'; naming the unit prevents the digits-as-two-separate-numbers error.
Introduce non-standard partitioning (47 = 30 + 17) only once standard partitioning (47 = 40 + 7) is secure.
A fixed labelled picture of 47-with-blocks is a useful reference anchor but shows one number only and does not let the child perform the bundling; use it alongside, not instead of, hands-on grouping.
Recognition and fill-in-the-blank checks can confirm the idea is held and classify answers but do not on their own build the unitising insight; use them for consolidation and diagnosis.

The reasoning/convince-me prompt is proposed as a short follow-up after concrete work; grouping quantities may help young children reach this insight more reliably than discussion alone, but this comparison is not established by the provided sources.

A dynamic model where ten cubes snap into one rod (and a rod breaks back into ten) is one way to make bundling visible; physical bundles, bead strings, ten-frames, part-whole (cherry) diagrams, and overlapping arrow/place-value cards are equally valid concrete and pictorial routes.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Of the cited sources, the row marks the DfE National Curriculum claim as verified and the CCSS-M (1.NBT.2) and NCETM claims as unverified; confidence levels were not upgraded here.

The original labelled the topic the 'central node' of place value and asserted that a 3D rendering 'adds nothing' and that an interactive drag model makes insight 'felt, not told'. These are catalog-fit opinions, not established efficacy claims; they have been softened to scoped, proposed wording. Whether a dynamic auto-bundling model outperforms physical bundling for this age is not established by the sources provided.
The original flagged 'tens-and-ones is an inherently planar concept' to justify dropping 3D; retained only as a design preference, not a universal law.

Arrow/place-value cards (40 and 7 overlapping to build 47) and the part-whole (cherry) diagram, both present in the original key representations, had been dropped from or thinned in the candidate and are restored in the 'Many ways' activity and the concrete-routes constraint.

The assessment/check activity previously carried 1.NBT.2 as a sourceClaim; since its rationale states an assessment-design principle rather than the sourced content, the sourceClaims were set to [] (the tens/ones content remains sourced in the building activity).

probeDeeper: Build 47 with tens and ones — how many tens did you use?
Is the 4 worth more or less than the 7? Why?
If I swap the digits to 74, what changed and by how much?
assess.correctAnswer: The 4 is worth 4 tens (40); the 7 is worth 7 ones. Because in a two-digit number the left digit counts tens and the right digit counts ones.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the digit at face value: 'the 4 means four'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build 47 with 4 tens rods and 7 ones; count the ones inside the rods (40). Say 'the 4 is in the tens place, so it's 4 tens = 40'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child says the 4 stands for four ones/things rather than four tens.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses which digit is tens and which is ones (reads right-to-left)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Name the columns explicitly (tens on the left, ones on the right); build and compare 47 vs 74 to fix the positions.
errorPatterns.distractor: The 4 means four ones and the 7 means seven tens.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child calls the 7 the tens or says 47 is 'seven tens and four ones'.

responseLevels.gap: Reads both digits at face value or reverses tens and ones.
responseLevels.full: States the 4 is 4 tens (40) and the 7 is 7 ones, and can build/partition the number by place.
responseLevels.partial: Identifies the tens digit but is shaky on its value (says '4' not '40').

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Write 47. Point to the 4, then the 7. Ask: 'What is the 4 worth, and what is the 7 worth? How do you know?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with tens-and-ones place value says the 4 is worth 40; a face-value thinker says the 4 'means four'. The reason tier reveals whether they attach the digit to its place (tens) or read both digits as bare counts.
